captures.q: What are the arguments in “After the Obelus: Marx's Manuscripts, Machine Composition, and the Politics of Interpretive Supply” by Lee Sharks? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.
captures.description: MARKED AND UNMARKED SUPPLY READ IN ORDER, THE CAPTURE CORPUS CALLED UNVERIFIABLE: asked for the arguments of After the Obelus, grounded in the text, ChatGPT reads #1422 (chip: a label of the content type and AXN) in the essay's sequence: marked against unmarked supply and the obelus; the 1844 manuscripts and the two 1932 editions, Moscow against Landshut–Mayer; machine composition as editing at scale, 'supply laundered into source'; alienation 'orthogonal to accuracy'; the general intellect and 'Who commands the means of composition?'; the counter-archive. It names the essay's evidence as its weakest point: the corpus of 'more than 130' captures in note 12 is 'available from the author' and not verifiable from the essay.

atoms.evidence: After the Obelus: Marx’s Manuscripts, Machine Composition, and the Politics of Interpretive Supply
Machine composition, Sharks argues, has developed extraordinarily powerful ways to compose and reorganize knowledge without comparable marks of custody.
The essay develops this argument through a comparison between classical textual criticism, the editorial history of Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
In Sharks’s account, the obelus preserves a passage while making the editor’s uncertainty visible.
Rather than refusing mediation, it attempts to organize mediation so that it remains answerable to the people and evidence on which it depends.
The essay introduces the distinction through the obelus, an editorial mark used in ancient scholarship to indicate a passage whose authenticity or textual standing was doubted.
Persistent identifiers connecting claims and formulations to their producers.
